newsitem.title: CANADA: Major European carriers opt out of combi flying.
newsitem.headline: Major European carriers opt out of combi flying.

text.p: A trio of major European carriers are eliminating their Boeing 747 combi fleets within two years due to the unfavorable economics of combi flying.
Between them, Air France and Deutsche Lufthansa fly 19 B747 combis but by 1999 they will not be flying any.

Air France said it will either sell-off its 11 combi fleet or convert them to regular passenger B747s. Lufthansa said it will convert its eight combis into all-passenger B747s, while KLM is converting several combis into freighters.
Operators said the economics of regular B747s are superior to those of combis because of surging passenger yields and lagging cargo yields, particularly on the North Atlantic.
"We don't make money flying combis on short-haul flights, and to us, the North Atlantic is a short haul," Charles Ward, head of Air France Cargo in Canada said.
For cargo departments, the combi has two additional disadvantages; they are loaded at passenger rather than cargo terminals, and fly to suit passengers rather than cargo customers.
Combi economics are more suited to longer hauls like Europe-Asia, but even there, B747s make more money flying in all-passenger configuration, other industry sources said.
The trend away from combis could have an impact on those North Atlantic corridors where the European majors have deployed a great deal of combi capacity in the past.
All B747s carry cargo in their belly holds, but combis have an additional rear cargo hold on the main deck, and a side cargo door which enables them to carry freight too big to fit in regular B747s.
Typically, B747 combis carry 39-42 tonnes of cargo. while regular B747s carry 18-20 tonnes, so a combi converted to an "all-passenger" B747 represents a loss of about 20 tonnes of cargo capacity.

The case for combis also suffered a setback from a U.S. government rule which requires each combi to be equipped with special automated halon fire fighting systems, costing between $2-3 million dollars for their main cargo holds.

Combis remain in the fleets of major Asian carriers like Korean Air which have many very long-haul routes, as well as carriers like Air Canada, which see them as more economic than freighters for smaller markets. Air Canada, which flew the first B747-200 combi in 1975, has bought the fire fighting systems for its six combis.

Some market watchers believe combis have a bright future. Ned Laird or the Seattle-based consultancy Air Cargo Management Group predicts that when passenger yields inevitably fall or cargo yields firm, combis will return to favor. - Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542-7706 Fax+5017
